_comment: Source-checked Florida classifications and a bounded South Florida pilot planting catalog. Verified dates record review of the linked evidence, not guarantees of plant identification or unchanged taxonomy.
source: Florida Native Plant Society profiles with UF/IFAS and Kew clarifications
scope: Florida nativity; preliminary school-landscape suggestions within the 330–334 ZIP pilot. Site suitability is conditional, not inferred from ZIP alone.
planning_method: Sun and moisture are conservatively simplified from each linked profile. Wet means consistently wet soil; occasional inundation alone is not mapped to wet. Space is a planning estimate from mature spread: small generally up to 4 ft, medium up to 10 ft, large above 10 ft; vines need managed support. Maintenance is an app planning estimate from growth and care notes, not an official rating. All new plantings need establishment care and school/facilities approval.
wildlife_method: Documented means a cited feeding, host or shelter relationship. It is neither a high/medium/low ranking nor a count of animals that will visit a site. Unknown indicates this catalog has not checked a relationship, not that the plant has no ecological value.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Coontie is the Atala butterfly's only Florida-native larval host. Atala caterpillars can also use some nonnative cycads; planting coontie does not guarantee their arrival.
species.suitability_notes: Slow-growing cycad, typically 3–5 ft wide. Use nursery-grown plants in well-drained soil. Seeds, foliage and roots are toxic; choose a school-approved location. Water during establishment.
species.taxonomy_notes: Zamia floridana is an older name for Florida coontie. Zamia pumila is not automatically merged: Kew accepts a separate Greater Antillean species under that name, while some Florida references use it differently.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Florida firebush offers nectar to hummingbirds and butterflies, while its fruits are eaten by birds and small mammals.
species.suitability_notes: Allow about 10 ft of mature width or plan selective pruning. Water until established. Obtain the Florida-native variety from a nursery that can confirm its identity.
species.taxonomy_notes: The unqualified species name does not distinguish the native variety from nonnative var. glabra. Confirm the variety before counting a photographed plant as native.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Muhly grass forms shelter for small animals, and small birds feed on its seeds.
species.suitability_notes: Clumps reach about 3.5 ft wide. Drought tolerance applies after establishment; irrigation needs depend on soil, weather and establishment. Occasional inundation tolerance is not a recommendation for continuously wet soil.
species.taxonomy_notes: The FNPS profile includes several infraspecific forms; nursery stock is commonly var. capillaris. Muhlenbergia filipes is not silently treated as an identical species.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: A larval host for monarch, queen and soldier butterflies; its flowers also attract bees and other pollinators.
species.suitability_notes: Typically 0.5–1.5 ft wide. Choose Florida-provenance stock and well-drained soil; establishment can be difficult. Seasonal dormancy is normal. Keep milkweed away from places where children or pets may ingest it.
species.taxonomy_notes: Kew explicitly records subsp. rolfsii as native to Florida and var. rolfsii/Asclepias rolfsii as synonyms. This survey aggregates those names at species level; it does not discard arbitrary subspecies.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Swamp milkweed is a host for monarch and queen caterpillars and a nectar resource for pollinators, including native bees.
species.suitability_notes: Typically 1.5–2 ft wide. Needs consistently moist to wet soil; do not substitute it into a dry bed. Seasonal dormancy is normal. Toxic if ingested; placement needs school review.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Saw palmetto is a host for monk and palmetto skippers and provides nectar for bees and butterflies.
species.suitability_notes: A spreading, clonal palm with sharp leaf stalks; allow up to 10 ft of width and keep away from walkways. Use nursery-grown plants and provide establishment water.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Flowers attract pollinators; seeds feed small mammals, and the palm offers nesting or roosting habitat to birds and bats.
species.suitability_notes: A large palm with a 10–20 ft crown. Fronds and flower stalks fall; facilities staff should approve placement and long-term care. Retaining habitat features depends on site safety.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Live oak hosts several butterfly caterpillars. Its acorns feed birds and mammals, and its branches provide nesting habitat.
species.suitability_notes: A long-lived tree with a potential 40–100 ft crown. Requires a large permanent planting area, utility clearance and facilities review; a small garden bed is unsuitable.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Sea grape flowers attract bees and butterflies; its fruit feeds birds and other wildlife.
species.suitability_notes: Can spread to about 35 ft wide. Coastal salt spray tolerance does not mean tolerance of flooding. Male and female plants are needed for fruit, and leaf litter needs space.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Buttonwood provides nectar and is a host for martial scrub-hairstreak and tantalus sphinx caterpillars.
species.suitability_notes: Potentially 20–40 ft wide as a tree. Confirm room, soil and intended pruning before choosing a hedge or tree form. Coastal occurrence alone does not establish suitability for a wet garden.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Red mangrove is a host for mangrove skipper caterpillars and provides cover for fish, birds and other animals in suitable shoreline habitat.
species.suitability_notes: Classification only: specialized shoreline habitat and protected mangrove management require qualified review. Excluded from ordinary school-garden recommendations.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Wild coffee flowers are nectar resources for butterflies and other pollinators; birds eat its fruit.
species.suitability_notes: Typically 1.5–3 ft wide. Suited to partial sun or shade; avoid constant full sun and prolonged dryness. Water until established. It is not a coffee substitute.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Cocoplum attracts pollinators, supplies fruit to birds and other wildlife, and forms dense cover.
species.suitability_notes: The species can reach 10–20 ft wide. Hedge size depends on the form and pruning; allow mature room instead of assuming every nursery cultivar stays small.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Beautyberry flowers attract pollinators and its fruits feed birds including catbirds, mockingbirds and robins.
species.suitability_notes: Typically 3–6 ft wide. Allow a natural shrub shape; seasonal cutback may improve form and flowering. Provide establishment water.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Gumbo limbo hosts dingy purplewing caterpillars, attracts insect pollinators, and produces fruit eaten by flycatchers.
species.suitability_notes: A large shade tree, often 20–30 ft wide and potentially wider. Plan permanent clearance and long-term tree care with facilities staff.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: A larval host for gulf fritillary, julia and zebra longwing butterflies; its flowers are pollinated by bees.
species.suitability_notes: A vine that can reach about 15 ft. Provide an approved trellis or managed groundcover space and monitor spreading growth. Allow caterpillars to eat leaves.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Tickseed flowers supply nectar and pollen to native bees, wasps and small butterflies.
species.suitability_notes: Typically 0.5–1.5 ft wide. Use a sunny, moist but unflooded bed. This annual or short-lived perennial reseeds, so plan seasonal management.

species.wildlife_support_basis: No species-specific wildlife relationship verified in this catalog.
species.why: A Florida-native clumping grass associated with wet prairies and marsh edges. This catalog has not verified a species-specific wildlife relationship.
species.suitability_notes: Classification only until wildlife benefit and site requirements receive a fuller review. Large clumps require space; occasional inundation does not mean permanently submerged planting.
species.taxonomy_notes: Kew accepts Sporobolus bakeri with Spartina bakeri as its synonym. Both resolve to the same survey taxon.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Fakahatchee grass is a host for several skipper butterflies and provides cover for small animals.
species.suitability_notes: Typically 2–4 ft wide and 4–6 ft tall. Useful in a moist planting area with room for upright clumps. Water until established; clean up cold-damaged growth as needed.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Yaupon flowers are visited by bees, and birds eat the fruits on female plants.
species.suitability_notes: Classification only in this South Florida pilot: the FNPS profile lists suitability through zone 10A, while pilot ZIP areas also include warmer zones. Female plants need a nearby male for fruit.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Simpson's stopper flowers attract bees and butterflies, and its fruits feed birds.
species.suitability_notes: Mature width varies from about 3 to 15 ft. Confirm the nursery form and allow room for suckers and seedlings; do not assume a small cultivar from species identity alone.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Frogfruit hosts common buckeye, phaon crescent and white peacock caterpillars and offers nectar to many butterflies.
species.suitability_notes: Low, spreading groundcover, about 6 inches tall. Use in low-traffic areas; it is not a play-field replacement. Edge the planting to manage spread and water during establishment.
